messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: City Council Member
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sensory Distraction: I put on loud music or TV, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Gregor Halvorsen is a 49-year-old married man of Norwegian-American descent who serves as a city council member in a mid-sized Midwestern municipality. He presented for psychological evaluation approximately eighteen months after returning from a National Guard deployment to a combat zone, reporting a PCL-5 score of 42 and describing a constellation of symptoms that had quietly dismantled the life he had worked decades to build.

During his deployment, Gregor's unit was ambushed during a routine supply convoy. The vehicle ahead of his was struck by an IED; the explosion was close enough that the concussive force threw him sideways in his seat. In the chaos that followed — smoke, screaming, the hands of a fellow soldier grabbing his shoulder to pull him from the wreckage — Gregor helped extract two injured men before the unit was able to secure the area. One of the men died before evacuation arrived. Gregor has never been able to reconstruct the full sequence of what happened between the initial blast and finding himself outside the vehicle. He reports that the memory feels like a film with entire scenes cut out, and when he tries to explain the event — to his wife, to his VA intake worker — he loses the thread entirely, trails off, and sometimes finds himself staring at the wall, unable to say where the words went. When recollection does come, it arrives not as narrative but as sensation: the terror he felt in those minutes returns with the same physiological force as the original event, his heart hammering, his breath shallow, as though the ambush is simply happening again.

It is this quality of his memory — fragmentary, unprocessed, and somatically charged — that has become the engine of his current distress. Because the account remains incomplete and cannot be told coherently, Gregor has come to believe there must be something catastrophically wrong with him, that a mind intact would be able to remember, to explain, to put it behind him. He monitors his own thoughts with exhausting vigilance, scanning for signs that he is, as he privately fears, losing his grip on sanity. The fragmented memory also keeps his nervous system in a state of unresolved alarm: without a clear beginning, middle, and end to the event, his body has never received the signal that it is over. Sleep is nearly impossible. He lies awake for hours, and on the nights he does drift off he wakes abruptly, certain something is wrong.

That certainty has hardened into a worldview. Gregor now operates from the conviction that the world is genuinely dangerous, that safety is a story other people tell themselves, and that his body — reacting as it does to every unexpected sound, every brush of contact — is simply telling the truth that others are too naive to hear. When a constituent touched his arm during a town hall meeting last spring to thank him for his service, Gregor lurched backward so visibly that it made the local paper's social column. Even when his wife holds his hand and tells him he is home, he cannot absorb it; the reassurance slides off something that has calcified inside him. These appraisals — that danger is everywhere, that his body is a reliable threat-detector rather than a dysregulated one — sustain his hypervigilance and keep his startle response on a hair trigger, which in turn pulls fragments of the ambush back to the surface: the hands on his shoulder, the smoke, the half-remembered faces. Each intrusion reinforces his certainty that he has not escaped anything, that the threat is ongoing, and the appraisals tighten further.

To manage the noise inside his head, Gregor has developed several strategies that have quietly made things worse. He fills every quiet moment with loud music or television, reasoning that if there is no silence there is no space for the memories to surface. He avoids all physical contact, having reorganized his public interactions and his marriage around a perimeter of untouchability. But the distraction and withdrawal prevent him from ever sitting with the memory long enough to process it, keeping it fragmented and therefore perpetually threatening. The avoidance, too, has fed his appraisal of himself as broken and of the world as a place requiring constant management.

Gregor came to seek help after his wife told him quietly that she felt she was living with a stranger. What he most fears is that she is right. What he most hopes is that someone can help him find the missing pieces — and that finding them will not destroy what remains.
